import math
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

PURDUE_GOLD = "#cfb991"
PURDUE_DARK_GOLD = "#8e6f3e"
PURDUE_BLACK = "#000000"
PURDUE_GRAY = "#6f727b"

plt.rcParams.update({
    "figure.dpi": 120,
    "axes.spines.top": False,
    "axes.spines.right": False,
    "axes.grid": True,
    "grid.alpha": 0.22,
})

Learning goals¶

After this lecture, you should be able to:

  • define convergence in terms of partial sums;

  • apply the preliminary, comparison, integral, ratio, limit-comparison, and alternating-series tests;

  • determine the radius and interval of convergence of a power series;

  • construct Taylor and Maclaurin series; and

  • estimate the error introduced by truncating a series.

Why series?¶

Series are used throughout mathematics, chemistry, and physics to:

  • represent functions using power, Taylor, and Fourier series;

  • construct approximate solutions to differential equations and integrals;

  • evaluate functions numerically; and

  • represent functions in a finite basis for computation.

The central questions are:

  • Do the partial sums approach a finite value? If so, the series converges; otherwise, it diverges.

  • If a series contains positive and negative terms, does it converge absolutely or only conditionally?

  • For a power series, what are its radius and interval of convergence?

  • When a convergent series is truncated, how large is the resulting error?

Infinite series and partial sums¶

An infinite series is a formal sum of infinitely many terms:

S=a1+a2+a3+⋯=∑n=1∞an.S=a_1+a_2+a_3+\cdots=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}a_n.S=a1​+a2​+a3​+⋯=n=1∑∞​an​.
(1)

Its NNN-th partial sum is

SN=∑n=1Nan.S_N=\sum_{n=1}^{N}a_n.SN​=n=1∑N​an​.
(2)

The series converges to SSS when the partial sums have the finite limit

S=lim⁡N→∞SN.S=\lim_{N\to\infty}S_N.S=N→∞lim​SN​.
(3)

If this finite limit does not exist, the series diverges. A divergent series may grow without bound, oscillate, or fail to settle to a single value in some other way.

The upper row below shows the terms ana_nan​; the lower row shows the corresponding partial sums SNS_NSN​. Convergence is a statement about the lower row, not merely about whether the terms in the upper row approach zero.

Source
n = np.arange(1, 31)
series_examples = [
    ("Geometric", 0.6 ** (n - 1), 1 / (1 - 0.6)),
    ("Harmonic", 1 / n, None),
    ("Alternating harmonic", (-1) ** (n - 1) / n, np.log(2)),
]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(11, 6), sharex="col")
for column, (title, terms, limit) in enumerate(series_examples):
    partial_sums = np.cumsum(terms)
    axes[0, column].stem(n, terms, linefmt=PURDUE_DARK_GOLD,
                         markerfmt="o", basefmt=" ")
    axes[0, column].set_title(title)
    axes[0, column].set_ylabel("$a_n$")
    axes[1, column].plot(n, partial_sums, "o-", color=PURDUE_DARK_GOLD,
                         markersize=3)
    if limit is not None:
        axes[1, column].axhline(limit, color=PURDUE_BLACK, linestyle="--",
                                linewidth=1.4, label=f"limit = {limit:.3f}")
        axes[1, column].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
    axes[1, column].set(xlabel="$N$", ylabel="$S_N$")

fig.suptitle("Terms and partial sums have different convergence stories", y=1.01)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

The geometric partial sums settle rapidly, the harmonic partial sums continue to grow, and the alternating-harmonic partial sums approach their limit from alternating sides.

Geometric series¶

A finite geometric series with first term aaa and common ratio rrr is

SN=a+ar+ar2+⋯+arN−1=∑n=0N−1arn.S_N=a+ar+ar^2+\cdots+ar^{N-1}=\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}ar^n.SN​=a+ar+ar2+⋯+arN−1=n=0∑N−1​arn.
(4)

For r≠1r\neq1r=1, multiply by rrr and subtract:

SN=a+ar+ar2+⋯+arN−1,rSN=ar+ar2+ar3+⋯+arN,(1−r)SN=a(1−rN).\begin{aligned} S_N &= a+ar+ar^2+\cdots+ar^{N-1},\\ rS_N &= ar+ar^2+ar^3+\cdots+ar^N,\\ (1-r)S_N &= a(1-r^N). \end{aligned}SN​rSN​(1−r)SN​​=a+ar+ar2+⋯+arN−1,=ar+ar2+ar3+⋯+arN,=a(1−rN).​
(5)

Therefore,

SN=a(1−rN)1−r.S_N=\frac{a(1-r^N)}{1-r}.SN​=1−ra(1−rN)​.
(6)

If ∣r∣<1|r|<1∣r∣<1, then rN→0r^N\to0rN→0, and the infinite geometric series converges:

∑n=0∞arn=a1−r,∣r∣<1.\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}ar^n=\frac{a}{1-r},\qquad |r|<1.n=0∑∞​arn=1−ra​,∣r∣<1.
(7)

For ∣r∣≥1|r|\geq1∣r∣≥1 and a≠0a\neq0a=0, the infinite geometric series does not converge.

For ∣r∣<1|r|<1∣r∣<1, truncating after NNN terms leaves another, smaller geometric series. The shaded bars visualize that remaining tail.

Source
r = 0.6
N_kept = 5
indices = np.arange(0, 15)
geometric_terms = r ** indices
tail_exact = r ** N_kept / (1 - r)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.8))
colors = [PURDUE_DARK_GOLD if k < N_kept else PURDUE_GOLD for k in indices]
ax.bar(indices, geometric_terms, color=colors, edgecolor="white")
ax.axvline(N_kept - 0.5, color=PURDUE_BLACK, linestyle="--", linewidth=1)
ax.text(1.4, 0.78, "terms retained", ha="center")
ax.text(8.0, 0.43,
        rf"remaining tail $=r^N/(1-r)={tail_exact:.4f}$",
        ha="center", color=PURDUE_DARK_GOLD)
ax.set(xlabel="$n$", ylabel="$r^n$",
       title=rf"A geometric series and its tail ($r={r}$, $N={N_kept}$)")
ax.set_xticks(indices[::2])
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

First convergence examples¶

Example 1: geometric growth

The series

1+2+4+8+16+⋯1+2+4+8+16+\cdots1+2+4+8+16+⋯
(8)

diverges. Its terms do not even approach zero.

Example 2: the harmonic series

The harmonic series

1+12+13+14+⋯1+\frac12+\frac13+\frac14+\cdots1+21​+31​+41​+⋯
(9)

diverges even though its terms approach zero. We will verify this with the integral test below.

Example 3: the alternating harmonic series

The alternating harmonic series

1−12+13−14+⋯1-\frac12+\frac13-\frac14+\cdots1−21​+31​−41​+⋯
(10)

converges to ln⁡2\ln 2ln2, but it does not converge absolutely. It is therefore conditionally convergent.

Interactive convergence explorer¶

Before interacting, predict which examples have terms that approach zero and which have partial sums that approach a finite value. Use the dropdown to change the series and the slider to increase the number of displayed terms.

Preliminary test for divergence¶

If ∑an\sum a_n∑an​ converges, then its terms must satisfy

lim⁡n→∞an=0.\lim_{n\to\infty}a_n=0.n→∞lim​an​=0.
(11)

Consequently, if this limit is nonzero or does not exist, the series diverges. The converse is false: an→0a_n\to0an​→0 does not by itself prove convergence.

Example

For the harmonic series, an=1/n→0a_n=1/n\to0an​=1/n→0, so the preliminary test is inconclusive. For

12+23+34+45+⋯ ,\frac12+\frac23+\frac34+\frac45+\cdots,21​+32​+43​+54​+⋯,
(12)

the terms approach 1, so the series diverges by the preliminary test.

The harmonic series demonstrates why the converse fails. Its individual terms approach zero, while its partial sums continue to grow approximately like ln⁡N\ln NlnN.

Source
n_harmonic = np.arange(1, 1001)
harmonic_terms = 1 / n_harmonic
harmonic_partial_sums = np.cumsum(harmonic_terms)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.8))
axes[0].plot(n_harmonic, harmonic_terms, color=PURDUE_DARK_GOLD, linewidth=2)
axes[0].set(xlabel="$n$", ylabel="$a_n=1/n$",
            title="The terms approach zero")

axes[1].plot(n_harmonic, harmonic_partial_sums, color=PURDUE_DARK_GOLD,
             linewidth=2, label="$S_N$")
axes[1].plot(n_harmonic, np.log(n_harmonic) + 0.5772156649015329, "k--",
             linewidth=1.3, label=r"$\ln N+\gamma$")
axes[1].set(xlabel="$N$", ylabel="$S_N$",
            title="The partial sums do not settle")
axes[1].legend(frameon=False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Direct comparison test¶

Suppose the terms are nonnegative for all sufficiently large nnn.

  • If 0≤an≤bn0\leq a_n\leq b_n0≤an​≤bn​ and ∑bn\sum b_n∑bn​ converges, then ∑an\sum a_n∑an​ converges.

  • If 0≤bn≤an0\leq b_n\leq a_n0≤bn​≤an​ and ∑bn\sum b_n∑bn​ diverges, then ∑an\sum a_n∑an​ diverges.

Warning

The direction of the inequality matters. Being smaller than the terms of a divergent series or larger than the terms of a convergent series gives no conclusion.

Example

For n≥1n\geq1n≥1, n!≥2n−1n!\geq2^{n-1}n!≥2n−1, so

0≤1n!≤12n−1.0\leq\frac{1}{n!}\leq\frac{1}{2^{n-1}}.0≤n!1​≤2n−11​.
(13)

Because ∑n=1∞2−(n−1)\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}2^{-(n-1)}∑n=1∞​2−(n−1) is a convergent geometric series, ∑n=1∞1/n!\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}1/n!∑n=1∞​1/n! converges by direct comparison.

Integral test¶

Let f(x)f(x)f(x) be continuous, positive, and decreasing for x≥Nx\geq Nx≥N, with an=f(n)a_n=f(n)an​=f(n). Then

∑n=N∞an\sum_{n=N}^{\infty}a_nn=N∑∞​an​
(14)

and

∫N∞f(x) dx\int_N^{\infty}f(x)\,dx∫N∞​f(x)dx
(15)

either both converge or both diverge.

Example: the harmonic series

For f(x)=1/xf(x)=1/xf(x)=1/x,

∫1Bdxx=ln⁡B.\int_1^B\frac{dx}{x}=\ln B.∫1B​xdx​=lnB.
(16)

Since ln⁡B→∞\ln B\to\inftylnB→∞ as B→∞B\to\inftyB→∞, the harmonic series diverges.

For the decreasing function f(x)=1/xf(x)=1/xf(x)=1/x, each left-endpoint rectangle lies above the curve. Extending the picture adds both rectangle area and integral area without bound.

Ratio test¶

For a series ∑an\sum a_n∑an​ with nonzero terms for sufficiently large nnn, let

L=lim⁡n→∞∣an+1an∣,L=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right|,L=n→∞lim​∣∣​an​an+1​​∣∣​,
(17)

provided the limit exists. Then:

  • if L<1L<1L<1, the series converges absolutely;

  • if L>1L>1L>1, or L=∞L=\inftyL=∞, the series diverges; and

  • if L=1L=1L=1, the test is inconclusive.

Example

For ∑n=0∞xn/n!\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}x^n/n!∑n=0∞​xn/n!,

∣an+1an∣=∣x∣n+1⟶0.\left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right| =\frac{|x|}{n+1}\longrightarrow0.∣∣​an​an+1​​∣∣​=n+1∣x∣​⟶0.
(18)

The series therefore converges absolutely for every real or complex xxx.

Limit-comparison test¶

Suppose an>0a_n>0an​>0, bn>0b_n>0bn​>0, and

lim⁡n→∞anbn=c,0<c<∞.\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{a_n}{b_n}=c, \qquad 0<c<\infty.n→∞lim​bn​an​​=c,0<c<∞.
(19)

Then ∑an\sum a_n∑an​ and ∑bn\sum b_n∑bn​ have the same convergence behavior.

Example

For

an=2n+1n3+4,bn=1n2,a_n=\frac{2n+1}{n^3+4},\qquad b_n=\frac{1}{n^2},an​=n3+42n+1​,bn​=n21​,
(20)

we have an/bn→2a_n/b_n\to2an​/bn​→2. Since ∑1/n2\sum 1/n^2∑1/n2 converges, so does ∑an\sum a_n∑an​.

Alternating series¶

An alternating series has the form

∑n=1∞(−1)n−1bn,bn≥0.\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(-1)^{n-1}b_n, \qquad b_n\geq0.n=1∑∞​(−1)n−1bn​,bn​≥0.
(21)

If bn+1≤bnb_{n+1}\leq b_nbn+1​≤bn​ for all sufficiently large nnn and bn→0b_n\to0bn​→0, the series converges.

A convergent series is absolutely convergent if ∑∣an∣\sum |a_n|∑∣an​∣ also converges. A series that converges but does not converge absolutely is conditionally convergent.

Note

The alternating harmonic series converges conditionally. Ionic-lattice sums provide a physical setting in which conditional convergence and the order or geometry of summation require special care.

For the alternating harmonic series, odd and even partial sums approach ln⁡2\ln 2ln2 from opposite sides. Consecutive partial sums bracket the exact value, and the bracket width is the magnitude of the next term.

Source
n_alternating = np.arange(1, 17)
alternating_terms = (-1) ** (n_alternating - 1) / n_alternating
alternating_partial_sums = np.cumsum(alternating_terms)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.2))
ax.plot(n_alternating, alternating_partial_sums, color=PURDUE_GRAY,
        linewidth=1.2, alpha=0.8)
odd = n_alternating % 2 == 1
ax.scatter(n_alternating[odd], alternating_partial_sums[odd],
           color=PURDUE_DARK_GOLD, s=45, label="odd partial sums")
ax.scatter(n_alternating[~odd], alternating_partial_sums[~odd],
           color=PURDUE_GOLD, edgecolor=PURDUE_DARK_GOLD, s=45,
           label="even partial sums")
ax.axhline(np.log(2), color=PURDUE_BLACK, linestyle="--", linewidth=1.5,
           label=r"$\ln 2$")
ax.fill_between(n_alternating,
                np.minimum(alternating_partial_sums,
                           np.r_[alternating_partial_sums[1:], np.log(2)]),
                np.maximum(alternating_partial_sums,
                           np.r_[alternating_partial_sums[1:], np.log(2)]),
                color=PURDUE_GOLD, alpha=0.16)
ax.set(xlabel="$N$", ylabel="$S_N$",
       title="Alternating partial sums bracket the limiting value")
ax.set_xticks(n_alternating)
ax.legend(frameon=False, ncol=3, fontsize=8)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Operations on convergent series¶

  • Multiplying every term by a fixed nonzero constant does not change whether a series converges, although it changes the sum.

  • Changing finitely many terms does not change convergence or divergence, although it may change the sum.

  • Two convergent series may be added or subtracted term by term, and their sums add or subtract correspondingly.

  • The terms of an absolutely convergent series may be rearranged without changing its sum. This is not generally true for a conditionally convergent series.

Power series¶

A power series centered at x=ax=ax=a has the form

∑n=0∞cn(x−a)n=c0+c1(x−a)+c2(x−a)2+⋯ .\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}c_n(x-a)^n =c_0+c_1(x-a)+c_2(x-a)^2+\cdots.n=0∑∞​cn​(x−a)n=c0​+c1​(x−a)+c2​(x−a)2+⋯.
(22)

Every power series has a radius of convergence RRR, where 0≤R≤∞0\leq R\leq\infty0≤R≤∞, such that it:

  • converges absolutely for ∣x−a∣<R|x-a|<R∣x−a∣<R;

  • diverges for ∣x−a∣>R|x-a|>R∣x−a∣>R; and

  • must be checked separately at the endpoints x=a±Rx=a\pm Rx=a±R when RRR is finite.

Example: radius and interval of convergence¶

Consider

∑n=0∞(−x)n2n=1−x2+x24−x38+⋯ .\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-x)^n}{2^n} =1-\frac{x}{2}+\frac{x^2}{4}-\frac{x^3}{8}+\cdots.n=0∑∞​2n(−x)n​=1−2x​+4x2​−8x3​+⋯.
(23)

The ratio test gives

L=∣x2∣.L=\left|\frac{x}{2}\right|.L=∣∣​2x​∣∣​.
(24)

Thus the radius of convergence is R=2R=2R=2. At x=2x=2x=2, the terms alternate between 1 and -1, so the series diverges. At x=−2x=-2x=−2, every term is 1, so the series also diverges. The interval of convergence is therefore (−2,2)(-2,2)(−2,2).

The radius determines the interior behavior, but it does not determine the endpoints. Two series can have the same radius and different endpoint results.

Source
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(9, 3.8), sharex=True)
endpoint_cases = [
    (r"$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(-x/2)^n$", "diverge", "diverge"),
    (r"$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(x/2)^n/n$", "converge", "diverge"),
]

for ax, (label, left_result, right_result) in zip(axes, endpoint_cases):
    ax.hlines(0, -3, -2, color="#b31b1b", linewidth=7, alpha=0.65)
    ax.hlines(0, -2, 2, color="#2e7d32", linewidth=7, alpha=0.7)
    ax.hlines(0, 2, 3, color="#b31b1b", linewidth=7, alpha=0.65)
    for location, result in [(-2, left_result), (2, right_result)]:
        if result == "converge":
            ax.scatter(location, 0, s=90, facecolor="#2e7d32",
                       edgecolor="white", linewidth=1.5, zorder=3)
        else:
            ax.scatter(location, 0, s=95, marker="x", color="#b31b1b",
                       linewidth=2.5, zorder=3)
        ax.text(location, 0.22, result, ha="center", fontsize=9)
    ax.text(-3.05, 0, label, ha="right", va="center")
    ax.set(ylim=(-0.32, 0.48), yticks=[])

axes[-1].set(xlim=(-3.2, 3.2), xticks=[-3, -2, 0, 2, 3], xlabel="$x$")
fig.suptitle("The interior follows the radius; endpoints require separate tests")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Algebra and calculus of power series¶

Inside the radius of convergence:

  • a power series may be differentiated or integrated term by term;

  • power series may be added, subtracted, and multiplied; and

  • one convergent power series may be substituted into another when the substituted values remain inside the outer series’ convergence interval.

Term-by-term differentiation and integration preserve the radius of convergence, but behavior at the endpoints must be checked again. A function’s power-series representation about a fixed center is unique wherever it exists.

Taylor and Maclaurin series¶

The Taylor series of f(x)f(x)f(x) about x=ax=ax=a is

f(x)=∑n=0∞f(n)(a)n!(x−a)n,f(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{f^{(n)}(a)}{n!}(x-a)^n,f(x)=n=0∑∞​n!f(n)(a)​(x−a)n,
(25)

when the series converges to f(x)f(x)f(x). The special case a=0a=0a=0 is the Maclaurin series:

f(x)=∑n=0∞f(n)(0)n!xn.f(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{f^{(n)}(0)}{n!}x^n.f(x)=n=0∑∞​n!f(n)(0)​xn.
(26)

For example, the derivatives of sin⁡x\sin xsinx cycle through sin⁡x,cos⁡x,−sin⁡x,−cos⁡x\sin x,\cos x,-\sin x,-\cos xsinx,cosx,−sinx,−cosx. Evaluating at x=0x=0x=0 gives

sin⁡x=x−x33!+x55!−⋯=∑n=0∞(−1)nx2n+1(2n+1)!.\sin x=x-\frac{x^3}{3!}+\frac{x^5}{5!}-\cdots =\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(-1)^n\frac{x^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!}.sinx=x−3!x3​+5!x5​−⋯=n=0∑∞​(−1)n(2n+1)!x2n+1​.
(27)

Maclaurin series to remember¶

ex=∑n=0∞xnn!=1+x+x22!+x33!+⋯ ,−∞<x<∞.e^x=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{n!} =1+x+\frac{x^2}{2!}+\frac{x^3}{3!}+\cdots, \qquad -\infty<x<\infty.ex=n=0∑∞​n!xn​=1+x+2!x2​+3!x3​+⋯,−∞<x<∞.
(28)
sin⁡x=∑n=0∞(−1)nx2n+1(2n+1)!,−∞<x<∞.\sin x=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(-1)^n\frac{x^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!}, \qquad -\infty<x<\infty.sinx=n=0∑∞​(−1)n(2n+1)!x2n+1​,−∞<x<∞.
(29)
cos⁡x=∑n=0∞(−1)nx2n(2n)!,−∞<x<∞.\cos x=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(-1)^n\frac{x^{2n}}{(2n)!}, \qquad -\infty<x<\infty.cosx=n=0∑∞​(−1)n(2n)!x2n​,−∞<x<∞.
(30)
11−x=∑n=0∞xn,∣x∣<1.\frac{1}{1-x}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}x^n, \qquad |x|<1.1−x1​=n=0∑∞​xn,∣x∣<1.
(31)
ln⁡(1+x)=∑n=1∞(−1)n+1xnn=x−x22+x33−⋯ ,−1<x≤1.\ln(1+x)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(-1)^{n+1}\frac{x^n}{n} =x-\frac{x^2}{2}+\frac{x^3}{3}-\cdots, \qquad -1<x\leq1.ln(1+x)=n=1∑∞​(−1)n+1nxn​=x−2x2​+3x3​−⋯,−1<x≤1.
(32)

For a general real or complex exponent ppp,

(1+x)p=∑n=0∞(pn)xn=1+px+p(p−1)2!x2+⋯ ,∣x∣<1.(1+x)^p =\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\binom{p}{n}x^n =1+px+\frac{p(p-1)}{2!}x^2+\cdots, \qquad |x|<1.(1+x)p=n=0∑∞​(np​)xn=1+px+2!p(p−1)​x2+⋯,∣x∣<1.
(33)

Endpoint behavior for the binomial series depends on ppp.

How to construct power-series expansions¶

Useful approaches include:

  1. Apply the Taylor formula by evaluating derivatives at the expansion point.

  2. Add, multiply, divide, differentiate, or integrate known power series.

  3. Substitute an expression into a known series while respecting its interval of convergence.

Examples worth practicing include excos⁡xe^x\cos xexcosx, tan⁡x\tan xtanx, and 1/(1−x)1/(1-x)1/(1−x). Since ln⁡x\ln xlnx is not analytic at x=0x=0x=0, expand it about x=1x=1x=1 by writing

ln⁡x=ln⁡ ⁣(1+(x−1)).\ln x=\ln\!\left(1+(x-1)\right).lnx=ln(1+(x−1)).
(34)

Taylor approximation and remainder¶

The degree-nnn Taylor polynomial about x=ax=ax=a is

Tn(x)=∑k=0nf(k)(a)k!(x−a)k.T_n(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{f^{(k)}(a)}{k!}(x-a)^k.Tn​(x)=k=0∑n​k!f(k)(a)​(x−a)k.
(35)

The remainder is

Rn(x)=f(x)−Tn(x).R_n(x)=f(x)-T_n(x).Rn​(x)=f(x)−Tn​(x).
(36)

Under the hypotheses of Taylor’s theorem, there is a point ccc between aaa and xxx such that

Rn(x)=f(n+1)(c)(n+1)!(x−a)n+1.R_n(x)=\frac{f^{(n+1)}(c)}{(n+1)!}(x-a)^{n+1}.Rn​(x)=(n+1)!f(n+1)(c)​(x−a)n+1.
(37)

If ∣f(n+1)(t)∣≤M|f^{(n+1)}(t)|\leq M∣f(n+1)(t)∣≤M between aaa and xxx, then

∣Rn(x)∣≤M∣x−a∣n+1(n+1)!.|R_n(x)|\leq\frac{M|x-a|^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}.∣Rn​(x)∣≤(n+1)!M∣x−a∣n+1​.
(38)

The Taylor series converges to f(x)f(x)f(x) at a point when Rn(x)→0R_n(x)\to0Rn​(x)→0.

Interactive Taylor approximation and error¶

Move the order slider and compare the approximation with the error. Before moving it, predict whether increasing the order will improve the approximation equally at every value of xxx.

Source
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

x_taylor = np.linspace(-3, 3, 500)
exp_exact = np.exp(x_taylor)
taylor_orders = list(range(0, 15))
initial_order = 4

def exponential_taylor(x_values, order):
    approximation = np.zeros_like(x_values, dtype=float)
    for power in range(order + 1):
        approximation += x_values**power / math.factorial(power)
    return approximation

taylor_figure = make_subplots(
    rows=1,
    cols=2,
    subplot_titles=("Function and Taylor polynomial", "Absolute error and bound"),
    horizontal_spacing=0.12,
)
taylor_figure.add_trace(
    go.Scatter(x=x_taylor, y=exp_exact, mode="lines", name="$e^x$",
               line=dict(color="#000000", dash="dash", width=2.5)),
    row=1,
    col=1,
)

for order in taylor_orders:
    approximation = exponential_taylor(x_taylor, order)
    absolute_error = np.maximum(np.abs(exp_exact - approximation), 1e-16)
    derivative_bound = np.where(x_taylor >= 0, np.exp(x_taylor), 1.0)
    lagrange_bound = np.maximum(
        derivative_bound * np.abs(x_taylor) ** (order + 1)
        / math.factorial(order + 1),
        1e-16,
    )
    visible = order == initial_order
    taylor_figure.add_trace(
        go.Scatter(x=x_taylor, y=approximation, mode="lines",
                   name=f"$T_{{{order}}}(x)$", visible=visible,
                   line=dict(color="#8e6f3e", width=3)),
        row=1,
        col=1,
    )
    taylor_figure.add_trace(
        go.Scatter(x=x_taylor, y=absolute_error, mode="lines",
                   name="actual error", visible=visible,
                   line=dict(color="#8e6f3e", width=2.5)),
        row=1,
        col=2,
    )
    taylor_figure.add_trace(
        go.Scatter(x=x_taylor, y=lagrange_bound, mode="lines",
                   name="Lagrange bound", visible=visible,
                   line=dict(color="#6f727b", dash="dot", width=2)),
        row=1,
        col=2,
    )

taylor_steps = []
for order_index, order in enumerate(taylor_orders):
    visibility = [True] + [False] * (3 * len(taylor_orders))
    trace_start = 1 + 3 * order_index
    visibility[trace_start:trace_start + 3] = [True, True, True]
    taylor_steps.append(
        dict(
            label=str(order),
            method="update",
            args=[
                {"visible": visibility},
                {"title": f"Maclaurin approximation to e^x: order N = {order}"},
            ],
        )
    )

taylor_figure.update_layout(
    title=f"Maclaurin approximation to e^x: order N = {initial_order}",
    template="plotly_white",
    height=520,
    margin=dict(t=100),
    sliders=[
        dict(
            active=taylor_orders.index(initial_order),
            currentvalue={"prefix": "Polynomial order N: "},
            pad={"t": 35},
            steps=taylor_steps,
        )
    ],
    legend=dict(orientation="h", yanchor="bottom", y=1.02,
                xanchor="right", x=1),
)
taylor_figure.update_xaxes(title_text="$x$")
taylor_figure.update_yaxes(title_text="value", row=1, col=1)
taylor_figure.update_yaxes(title_text="absolute error", type="log", row=1, col=2)
taylor_figure.show()
Loading...

The approximation typically improves fastest near the expansion center. The error panel also distinguishes the actual error from a rigorous upper bound; the bound need not be tight to be valid.

The following static overview compresses the same idea into one image. Darker regions indicate smaller errors.

Source
error_orders = np.arange(0, 17)
error_grid = np.empty((len(error_orders), len(x_taylor)))
for row, order in enumerate(error_orders):
    approximation = exponential_taylor(x_taylor, int(order))
    error_grid[row] = np.maximum(np.abs(exp_exact - approximation), 1e-16)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.5))
image = ax.imshow(
    np.log10(error_grid),
    origin="lower",
    aspect="auto",
    extent=[x_taylor.min(), x_taylor.max(), error_orders.min(), error_orders.max()],
    cmap="viridis",
    vmin=-12,
    vmax=1,
)
colorbar = fig.colorbar(image, ax=ax)
colorbar.set_label(r"$\log_{10}|e^x-T_N(x)|$")
ax.set(xlabel="$x$", ylabel="Taylor order $N$",
       title="Taylor error depends on order and distance from the center")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Error bounds for series¶

For an alternating series

S=∑k=0∞(−1)kbkS=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(-1)^k b_kS=k=0∑∞​(−1)kbk​
(39)

with bk≥0b_k\geq0bk​≥0, bk+1≤bkb_{k+1}\leq b_kbk+1​≤bk​, and bk→0b_k\to0bk​→0, the error after terms through k=Nk=Nk=N satisfies

∣S−∑k=0N(−1)kbk∣≤bN+1.\left|S-\sum_{k=0}^{N}(-1)^k b_k\right|\leq b_{N+1}.∣∣​S−k=0∑N​(−1)kbk​∣∣​≤bN+1​.
(40)

For a power series tail with coefficients satisfying ∣cn+1∣≤∣cn∣|c_{n+1}|\leq|c_n|∣cn+1​∣≤∣cn​∣ for n≥N+1n\geq N+1n≥N+1 and ∣x∣<1|x|<1∣x∣<1, comparison with a geometric series gives

∣∑n=N+1∞cnxn∣≤∣cN+1xN+1∣1−∣x∣.\left|\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}c_nx^n\right| \leq\frac{|c_{N+1}x^{N+1}|}{1-|x|}.∣∣​n=N+1∑∞​cn​xn∣∣​≤1−∣x∣∣cN+1​xN+1∣​.
(41)

Numerical uses and limits¶

Series can be used for numerical evaluation, differentiation, integration, and limits. For example,

sin⁡xx=1−x23!+x45!−⋯ ,\frac{\sin x}{x} =1-\frac{x^2}{3!}+\frac{x^4}{5!}-\cdots,xsinx​=1−3!x2​+5!x4​−⋯,
(42)

so

lim⁡x→0sin⁡xx=1.\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin x}{x}=1.x→0lim​xsinx​=1.
(43)

L’Hopital’s rule provides an alternative for appropriate indeterminate forms, but it requires its own hypotheses; it is not a consequence of this single example.

Further visual investigations¶

The visualizations in this section reinforce useful ideas but are not required for the main path through the lecture. They are collected here so their value can be assessed after the core material has been taught.

A direct-comparison envelope¶

The comparison 1/n!≤1/2n−11/n!\leq 1/2^{n-1}1/n!≤1/2n−1 becomes especially clear on a logarithmic scale. The smaller positive series is trapped beneath a known convergent geometric series.

Source
n_comparison = np.arange(1, 13)
factorial_terms = np.array([1 / math.factorial(int(k)) for k in n_comparison])
geometric_bound = 1 / 2 ** (n_comparison - 1)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.9))
ax.semilogy(n_comparison, factorial_terms, "o-", color=PURDUE_DARK_GOLD,
            linewidth=2.2, label="$1/n!$")
ax.semilogy(n_comparison, geometric_bound, "s--", color=PURDUE_BLACK,
            linewidth=1.7, label="$1/2^{n-1}$")
ax.fill_between(n_comparison, factorial_terms, geometric_bound,
                color=PURDUE_GOLD, alpha=0.25)
ax.set(xlabel="$n$", ylabel="term magnitude (log scale)",
       title="A convergent geometric series bounds $1/n!$ from above")
ax.set_xticks(n_comparison)
ax.legend(frameon=False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Approaching the radius of convergence¶

For ∑n=0∞(−x/2)n\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(-x/2)^n∑n=0∞​(−x/2)n, convergence becomes slower near ∣x∣=2|x|=2∣x∣=2 and fails outside that radius.

Source
partial_sum_indices = np.arange(1, 36)
x_choices = [1.5, 1.9, 2.1]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.2))
for x_choice, color in zip(x_choices,
                           [PURDUE_DARK_GOLD, PURDUE_GOLD, PURDUE_GRAY]):
    powers = np.arange(0, len(partial_sum_indices))
    partial_sums = np.cumsum((-x_choice / 2) ** powers)
    ax.plot(partial_sum_indices, partial_sums, "o-", markersize=3,
            linewidth=1.7, color=color, label=rf"$x={x_choice}$")
    if abs(x_choice) < 2:
        ax.axhline(1 / (1 + x_choice / 2), color=color,
                   linestyle="--", linewidth=1, alpha=0.8)

ax.set(xlabel="$N$", ylabel="$S_N(x)$",
       title="Partial sums inside, near, and outside the radius $R=2$")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
Additional interactive ideas retained for later

  • Make the number of integral-test rectangles adjustable. The static diagram may already communicate the idea adequately.

  • Add a short “choose the convergence test” activity with feedback. This is probably better placed with homework or review questions than in the main exposition.

  • Let students rearrange positive and negative blocks of the alternating harmonic series. This is mathematically valuable but belongs after students are comfortable with conditional convergence.

  • A freehand sequence or function-drawing tool was considered but is not recommended here: deciding convergence from an arbitrary sketch would be ambiguous and could reinforce incorrect reasoning.

    1. ∑n=1∞(−1)nxnn(n+1)\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{(- 1)^n x^n}{n(n+1)}∑n=1∞​n(n+1)(−1)nxn​

For the following series: a) find the first few terms of the Maclaurin series for each of the following functions; b) Find the general term and write the series in summation form; c) check your results in (a) by computer; d) use a computer to plot the function and several approximating partial sums of the series.

    1. xsin⁡x\frac{x}{\sin x}sinxx​

    3. cos⁡(ex−1)\cos(e^x - 1)cos(ex−1)

  4. Find the first few terms of the Taylor series for the following functions about the given points.

    1. f(x)=cos⁡x,  a=πf(x) = \cos x , \; a = \pif(x)=cosx,a=π

    2. f(x)=ex,  a=5f(x) = e^x , \; a = 5f(x)=ex,a=5

  5. Read about issues in numerical evaluations of small-value expressions in Example 1 in Section 1.15 (page 56).

  6. Suppose a large number of particles are bouncing back and forth between x = 0 and x = 1, except that at each endpoint some escape. Let r be the fraction reflected each time; then (1 - r) is the fraction escaping. Suppose the particles start at x = 0 heading toward x = 1; eventually all particles will escape. Write an infinite series for the fraction which escape at x = 1 and similarly for the fraction which escape at x = 0. Sum both the series. What is the largest fraction of the particles which can escape at x = 0? (Remember that r must be between 0 and 1.)

  7. In a water purification process, one-nth of the impurity is removed in the first stage. In each succeeding stage, the amount of impurity removed is one-nth of that removed in the preceding stage. Show that if n = 2, the water can be made as pure as you like, but that if n = 3, at least one-half of the impurity will remain no matter how many stages are used.

  8. In classical mechanics, kinetic energy is given by K=p22mK = \frac{p^2}{2m}K=2mp2​ where ppp is the momentum. However, Einstein’s theory of relativity showed that this expression is just an approximation valid for velocities v≪cv \ll cv≪c, where c≈299,792,458c \approx 299,792,458c≈299,792,458 m/s. In special relativity, the total energy of a particle includes both its kinetic energy and rest energy, with the total energy E given by:

E=p2c2+m2c4E = \sqrt{p^2c^2 + m^2c^4}E=p2c2+m2c4​
(44)
Here, $m$ is the rest mass of the particle, and $p$ is its relativistic momentum. The rest energy of the particle (when p = 0) is given by $E_{rest} = mc^2$. Perform a Taylor series expansion of the total energy expression $E$ in terms of the small parameter $v/c$, assuming that the rest mass energy dominates over the kinetic energy. Expand up to second order in $v/c$ to obtain the next-order correction to the total energy in the low-velocity limit.

ChatGPT-assisted extensions¶

For any of these assignments, students may use ChatGPT as a provisional collaborator, but the submission must include the important prompts, an independent mathematical check, at least one correction or limitation, and the student’s own conceptual explanation. ChatGPT output by itself is not evidence.

  1. Convergence-test referee. Ask ChatGPT to classify six carefully chosen series, including a boundary case, a conditionally convergent series, and a series whose terms approach zero but whose partial sums diverge. Check every classification from the definitions or a justified test, then write a referee report identifying the first unsupported step. The conceptual goal is to distinguish necessary conditions from sufficient tests.

  2. Design a deceptive series. Use ChatGPT to propose a series that looks convergent from its first 50 partial sums but is actually divergent, or looks divergent initially but converges. Plot enough terms and partial sums to reveal the trap, prove the true behavior, and explain why finite numerical evidence cannot establish an infinite limiting claim.

  3. Taylor guarantee challenge. Choose a physically meaningful function, such as a Boltzmann factor or a short-time exponential decay. Ask ChatGPT for a Taylor approximation that meets a specified accuracy on an interval. Verify the coefficients, test the claimed error numerically, and derive a remainder bound that actually guarantees the tolerance. Explain why the expansion point and interval matter.
